description: A reference of common architecture styles with example layouts, trade-offs and when each fits. Used by `governance architecture` to explain what a repository looks like and what it could follow. It is advice, not a standard: the governance standards decide what is required, this only describes options. Where a style has a bundled architecture profile, `check --profile` can enforce its dependency rules.

styles.name: Simple monolith
styles.summary: One deployable with little internal structure: code is grouped by what is convenient. The right starting point for a small or exploratory project.
strengths: Fastest to start and easy to run, debug and deploy
No abstractions to maintain before they are needed
weaknesses: Coupling grows unnoticed; nothing stops any file using any other
Boundaries are hard to find and cut later
bestWhen: A prototype, a small tool or an early product
One or two developers and a domain that is still being learned
Roughly under 40 source files
avoidWhen: Several teams change it at once
It must live for years or is regulated
firstSteps: Keep input and output (HTTP, files, database) out of the functions that decide things
When folders start to be needed, name them by concern and move to a layered or modular layout

styles.name: Layered (n-tier)
styles.summary: Code is split by technical role into presentation, business logic and data access, and each layer may only call the one below it.
strengths: Familiar to almost every developer, so onboarding is quick
A good fit for CRUD-style applications
Simple to reason about at small and medium size
weaknesses: Layers are organised by technology, so one feature change touches every layer
Business rules tend to leak into controllers and database code
The business layer ends up depending on persistence details
bestWhen: CRUD-heavy back ends and internal tools
Small and medium teams with a stable, well-understood domain
avoidWhen: Complex business rules that must not depend on a database or framework
Many independent features that different teams own
firstSteps: Make dependencies one-way: controllers call services, services call repositories, never the reverse
Do not query the database from controllers
Pass plain data objects between layers instead of database rows

styles.name: MVC (Model, View, Controller)
styles.summary: A web-application pattern: models hold data and rules, views render output, controllers handle requests and connect the two. Most server-rendered frameworks are built around it.
strengths: Native to frameworks such as Rails, Django, Laravel and Spring MVC, so tooling and conventions help
Clear separation of rendering from request handling
weaknesses: Fat controllers and fat models are common
Says nothing about how a large domain is divided, so it strains as the application grows
bestWhen: Server-rendered websites and admin tools
Teams that want the conventions of an MVC framework
avoidWhen: The user interface is a separate single-page app talking to an API
The domain logic is large and needs to be independent of the web framework
firstSteps: Keep controllers thin: parse the request, call one function, choose a response
Move rules that are not about persistence out of models into plain services

styles.name: Clean Architecture (Onion)
styles.summary: Business rules sit in the middle and depend on nothing. Use cases surround them, and frameworks, databases and the web sit on the outside. Dependencies point inward only.
structure: domain/          (entities and business rules; imports nothing outward)
strengths: Business logic can be tested without a database, a web server or a framework
Frameworks and databases can be replaced with limited impact
The dependency rule can be checked mechanically
weaknesses: More files and mapping code than a layered design
Overkill for simple CRUD
Only works if the team keeps the discipline
bestWhen: A rich domain with real business rules
A product that will live for years and outlast its framework
firstSteps: Create the domain folder first and forbid it from importing anything from the other folders
Put each user action in one use case that takes and returns plain data
Enforce the rule with `governance check --profile 22-governance-operations/model/architecture-profile-clean-architecture.json`

styles.name: Hexagonal (Ports and Adapters)
styles.summary: The application core defines ports (interfaces) for what it offers and what it needs. Adapters on the outside, such as a REST controller, a queue consumer or a database, plug into those ports.
strengths: Many ways in (API, queue, CLI) and many things out (database, third parties) stay interchangeable
The core is testable with simple fakes for each port
The dependency rule can be checked mechanically
weaknesses: Interface and wiring overhead
Easy to create ports that only have one implementation and no value
bestWhen: Several inbound channels or several outbound integrations
Integration-heavy services where external systems change often
avoidWhen: A small CRUD application with one database and one interface
firstSteps: Define one outbound port per external dependency the core needs (storage, payments, email)
Keep adapters free of business rules
Enforce the rule with `governance check --profile 22-governance-operations/model/architecture-profile-hexagonal.json`

styles.name: Modular monolith
styles.summary: One deployable, divided into feature modules with strict boundaries. Each module owns its logic and data and talks to others only through a small public interface.
structure: orders/     (its own logic, data and public API)
strengths: Strong boundaries without the cost of running distributed services
Simple to deploy, debug and test end to end
Modules that need it can be split out into services later
weaknesses: Needs discipline to stop modules reaching into each other
A shared database makes it tempting to cross boundaries
bestWhen: A medium to large product with several distinct features
Several teams working in one codebase
You want boundaries now but are not ready for microservices
avoidWhen: A very small application, where the module overhead is not repaid
firstSteps: Identify two or three business capabilities and give each a folder with one public entry point
Forbid importing another module's internals; allow only its public interface
Adapt the example profile `architecture-profile-modular-example.json` to your module names and enforce it

styles.name: Microservices
styles.summary: The system is a set of small services, each deployed on its own, owning its data and communicating over the network.
structure: orders/       (own code, own database, own Dockerfile)
strengths: Teams can build, deploy and scale their services independently
A failure can be contained to one service
Different services can use different technology
weaknesses: Distributed-systems complexity: network failures, data consistency, versioning, tracing
High operational cost: pipelines, monitoring and deployment for every service
Wrong boundaries produce a distributed monolith, which is worse than a monolith
bestWhen: Several autonomous teams and clear business boundaries
Parts of the system have very different scaling needs
Mature automation and monitoring are already in place
avoidWhen: A small team or an early product whose boundaries are still moving
Services would share one database or must always be released together
firstSteps: Give each service its own data store and its own pipeline before adding more services
Put contracts (OpenAPI or protobuf) in version control and test against them
Enforce the rule with `governance check --profile 22-governance-operations/model/architecture-profile-microservices.json`

styles.name: Event-driven
styles.summary: Components communicate by publishing and reacting to events through a broker instead of calling each other directly. Often combined with CQRS or event sourcing.
strengths: Producers and consumers are decoupled and can scale separately
Absorbs traffic spikes and suits workflows that span services
The event stream is a natural audit trail
weaknesses: Harder to trace and debug than a direct call
Eventual consistency, ordering and duplicate delivery must be handled
Event contracts need versioning
bestWhen: Workflows that cross several services or systems
Integration-heavy systems and asynchronous processing
avoidWhen: The team has no experience with brokers or eventual consistency
firstSteps: Make consumers idempotent so a repeated event does no harm
Version every event schema and keep it in one place
Add a correlation id to every event so a flow can be traced

styles.name: Serverless (functions)
styles.summary: The application is a set of functions run on demand by a cloud platform, triggered by requests or events, with no servers to manage.
structure: serverless.yml    (or SAM, Netlify, Vercel or Firebase configuration)
strengths: No servers to operate and you pay for use
Scales automatically, down to zero
Quick to ship small, event-driven features
weaknesses: Cold starts, execution time limits and platform-specific behaviour
Vendor lock-in and harder local testing
Costs can exceed a server at steady high load
bestWhen: Spiky or occasional workloads, glue code and small APIs
Small teams that do not want to run infrastructure
avoidWhen: A steady heavy load where a server is cheaper
firstSteps: Keep each function small and stateless, and share logic through a library
Put infrastructure in code (serverless.yml, SAM or CDK) and review it
Set timeouts and concurrency limits on every function
